en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Transcending Difficulties, translated by the Western Jin lay devotee Nie Chengyuan.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī with the venerable Śakuna.

At that time, there was in the country a householder of the four castes named Vairaṭa, who was immensely wealthy and possessed a great abundance of rare jewels, precious gems, cattle, horses, fields, and houses.
He was stingy, greedy, and envious toward others, having no faith in the Way and its Virtue, nor did he delight in giving.
Before the sun had even set, he would constantly command his gatekeeper: "Should anyone come to beg, do not let them pass."
Dhana had an only son named Candana, who was likewise stingy and greedy.
After Dhana’s life came to an end, he was reborn in that same country as the son of a blind beggar woman.
Her husband said, "Your body is afflicted with a grave illness, and now you are pregnant again. I am so poor that I have nothing for food or clothing; you had better leave on your own.
Following these instructions, the wife went outside the gate; not far from there, she came upon a large heap of dung and stopped there in the midst of it.
In the ninth month, he gave birth to a son whose two eyes were blind; his mother went begging for food to nourish him.
When the boy reached the age of seven, his mother said:
"I have raised you for a very long time; from now on, go out yourself with a staff, take a begging bowl, and go begging, while reciting these words of self-pity:..."
"Among those in the world, the poor suffer the most.
Now, I, of meager fortune, was born into a poor family; moreover, my two eyes are blind so that I see nothing, and I am further treated with contempt by others."
"Now there is one who begs from me for a little food and drink to satisfy my hunger; it is like rain falling from heaven, so that the thirsty may find a drink.
When the son heard his mother speak thus, he went from house to house begging and eventually arrived at the house of Candana.
Just as her son arrived, the gatekeeper happened to step out briefly, whereupon the blind boy went straight in and reached the middle courtyard, speaking exactly as his mother had instructed.
At that time, Candana, who was atop a high tower, heard his words and became greatly incensed;
she called out to the gatekeeper and asked, "Who let this blind beggar inside?"

The gatekeeper was seized with great terror; he immediately dragged the blind boy and dashed him against the threshold outside the gate, injuring his head and face, breaking his right arm, and shattering his eating vessels. The rice was scattered across the ground, and the boy’s body suffered intense pain.
The child cried out piteously; hearing this, his mother immediately rushed to where he was and said:
"What kind of wretched person is tormenting my son?
My son is still small and both his eyes are blind; what fault has he committed that such a thing should be done to him?"
"What has so moved Heaven?
The son replied to his mother:

"While I was begging at this gate, there was a man with a loud voice who called out for 'Strong Man' (Tou-li) to pull me down and strike me, wounding me so that my body is in great pain like this; I shall likely die before long."
At that time, there was a guardian deity above the gate who spoke to him, saying:
"The pain you have now is but minor; the greater part is yet to come.
You sit here suffering because in a previous life you possessed wealth but failed to practice generosity."
Worldly wealth and status are not permanent; to possess wealth and status yet fail to practice generosity is equivalent to being destitute.
When death brings further suffering and one then falls into grief and regret, what benefit will it be?
At that time, the spectators were very numerous, each speaking to one another so that their voices were heard from afar.
Then the Buddha, awakening from his meditative contemplation of the Path, entered the city together with the bhikṣus to beg for alms.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"What kind of sound is this?
Why is it so sudden and urgent?"
Ānanda then addressed the Buddha, having related the past life of the mother of the blind son; he then joined his palms and said to the Buddha:
"I pray that you will have compassion and pity, and come to where this child is."
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
After returning from his alms round and finishing his meal, he went to visit him.

Seeing that the blind boy was suffering from the pain of his wound, the Buddha stroked the boy’s head with his hand; immediately, the boy’s eyes opened and his broken injuries were healed. Thereupon, the boy recognized his own past lives.
The Buddha asked,
"Are you the elder named Nanda from your previous life? He replied:
"Yes," [he replied].
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"People dwelling in this world undergo great toil and suffering in their folly; within a single lifetime, fathers and sons do not even recognize one another."
At that time, the Buddha spoke this sutra to resolve their thoughts:
"People who seek sons or search for wealth undergo great anxiety,
toil, and suffering in these two matters, yet it is another who reaps the fruit."
One cannot preserve even this body, let alone one's children or wealth.
It is like the heat of a summer month; one finds cool relief by resting beneath a tree, but in a moment it must pass away—there is nothing permanent in the world.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"When this child's life comes to an end, to which realm will he go?
The Buddha said:
"You shall dwell for one night within the great Avīci hell.
When the Buddha spoke this sutra, more than eighty thousand people cast off the three impurities and attained the Dharma-eye.
All the disciples rejoiced, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Transcending Difficulties
